name: Pinellia rhizome (Banxia in Chinese, Hange in Japanese, Banha in Korean)
short: Pregnancy: no study in pregnant women; embryo deaths in rats; mouse embryo protein changes suggest nervous-system harm. Japan reports: lung-disease signal. Cases: poisoning (title only), work asthma.
text: Pinellia rhizome is an East Asian herbal medicine, known as Banxia in Chinese, Hange in Japanese and Banha in Korean. No study reporting adverse events in people taking the herb on its own by mouth was found (an analysis of Japanese adverse-event reports on herbal medicines is described below), and a 2025 systematic review describes clinical safety data on it as scarce. Human reports: a 2010 case report, available as a title only, describes one case of poisoning with raw Pinellia ternata (the title does not give the route or outcome); and two case reports describe occupational asthma caused by the herb (Banha), in which a bronchial challenge test with the herb caused an early asthmatic response; one found IgE antibodies to the herb and the other did not (exposure at work, not taken by mouth). Lungs (reporting data): in an analysis of Japan's adverse-drug-event report database (830,079 reports, April 2004 to April 2023), daily intake of Pinellia tuber (hange in Japanese), one of three herbal drugs studied, was associated with reports of drug-induced interstitial lung disease, which the authors describe as a severe adverse event leading to morbidity and mortality, with an adjusted reporting odds ratio of 1.05 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.10) for its daily intake (the abstract does not give the unit of intake), and the authors conclude that the lung disease was dose-dependent on the crude drugs; reporting signals were found for 32 of 54 herbal medicines, including Pinellia tuber. Reports of this kind cannot show cause or how often it happens, and the abstract does not say which products contained the herb. Reviews (cautions, mostly from animal and laboratory work): one states that the raw rhizome cannot be taken by mouth before processing and lists among its toxic effects death in animals, inflammation, conjunctival irritation, pregnancy toxicity, teratogenicity, visceral toxicity, loss of voice (aphonia) and vomiting; another says the raw tuber causes acrid irritation of the mouth and throat when taken by mistake and that proper processing greatly reduces its toxicity; a third lists irritant toxicity, cardiotoxicity, hepatotoxicity and embryonic toxicity and says processing and combination with other herbs can reduce them; and the 2025 review reports that metabonomic studies suggest the raw rhizome may show cardiotoxicity and pregnancy toxicity but no apparent liver or kidney toxicity. Pregnancy: no study in pregnant women was found. In pregnant rats, crude Pinellia powder increased vaginal bleeding and embryo deaths, processed powder at the same dose showed no toxicity, and a decoction of processed or crude rhizome at a higher dose increased both (animal data). In pregnant mice given raw Pinellia by mouth on days 6 to 8 of gestation, the abundance of many embryonic proteins changed, and the functions of 37 of the changed proteins were mainly related to nervous-system development; the authors suggest that it may cause abnormalities of the fetal nervous system, and they note that the herb is commonly prescribed for vomiting in pregnant women (animal data). In pregnant rats given Pinellia root (Banxia) as a suspension or a processed product (Jiang Banxia) as a decoction, by mouth, the weight and histology of the placenta showed no definite difference between groups, but 20 metabolites in the placenta and amniotic fluid changed significantly; the authors say that data on the safety of its processed products for pregnant women are contradictory and confusing (animal data). A 2003 review, available as a title only, concerns studies of anti-early-pregnancy effects of Pinellia protein; the title does not say in what species or with what results. A 2022 review names Rhizoma Pinelliae among traditional Chinese medicines reported to cause reproductive toxicity in humans and animals, without separate details in its abstract. Interactions (animal data only): in rats, raw and processed Pinellia rhizome inhibited the drug-metabolising enzyme CYP3A, and the authors suggest that taking it with other drugs cleared by CYP3A may cause interactions; no human interaction data were found.
